Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

harnessr 0.6.0.9000

Renamed

  • The package is now called harnessr. readgpt grew a general core for model calls (clients, spending limits, a response cache, recordings that replay offline, traces) under its document-reading layer, and the new name says so. Load it with library(harnessr). The GitHub repository is renamed to elkronos/harnessr too, and GitHub sends the old address there, so remotes::install_github("elkronos/harnessr") installs it and the old elkronos/readgpt still works. The website moves to https://elkronos.github.io/harnessr/. No exported function, class, argument or prompt changes name in this release except readgpt_example(), below.

  • readgpt_example() is now gr_example(), which returns the same path to the bundled example document. readgpt_example() still works, with one gr_deprecated warning per session naming the new function.

  • Requests, cache keys and recordings are unchanged by the rename. Every request is sent as 0.6.0 sent it, and the corpus store key is the one 0.6.0 computed. The response-cache and replay keys change later in this release (see “Cache and replay keys” below), and the keys 0.6.0 computed are still looked up, so a warm cache, a recording made for gr_replay_client() and a gr_read_many() store all keep answering.

  • Two options are renamed: readgpt.api_key is now harnessr.api_key, and readgpt.allow_local_urls is now harnessr.allow_local_urls. The old names are still read when the new ones are not set, with one gr_deprecated warning per session naming the new option.

  • The help pages now suggest tools::R_user_dir("harnessr", "cache") for a cache that lasts. With that directory set, entries readgpt kept in tools::R_user_dir("readgpt", "cache") are read too, after it; new entries are written only to the new directory, and the old one is never cleared. The per-session default is now file.path(tempdir(), "harnessr-cache").

  • Text that named the package now says harnessr: the URL fetcher’s user agent (harnessr/<version>), the audit report’s title and footer, messages, and the Shiny app’s title. A trace’s meta still records the version under readgpt, so traces written before and after the rename read the same way.

Traces record what was sent and what came back

  • Each request step records params_sent, the request as it went out with every default resolved: the model, api, base_url, the output cap actually sent (a reasoning model’s small cap goes out raised to 2048), the temperature (filled from gr_options("temperature"), or NA when none was sent), the effort, the schema name, and SHA-256 hashes of the schema and of the extra body fields. For a gr_client() it is read from the request body itself. params keeps what the caller asked for, as before. Requests, response-cache keys and replay keys are unchanged.

  • Steps record served_model, response_id and fingerprint where the provider returns them, beside model, which stays the model asked for and is what a step is priced and replayed by. None of them enters a cache or replay key. gr_call() results carry the same three fields.

  • Steps record attempts, the number of requests sent, retries included (0 for a reply from a cache or a recording), and started_utc and ended_utc as ISO 8601 in UTC with a trailing Z. A saved trace’s started is now written in UTC with a Z too; it was local time with no offset.

  • Token records say where they came from. A step’s tokens gains provenance: "reported" by the provider, "counted" here with the "tiktoken" tokenizer, or "estimated" with another one. Reasoning and cached input tokens the provider reports are kept as tokens$reasoning and tokens$cached_input, parts of output and input rather than additions. gr_trace_summary() gains tokens_reasoning, tokens_cached_in and usage_estimated, the share of requests whose counts were estimated, and print() on a trace says that share when it is above zero. A request that failed before the provider sent any usage records a "counted" zero, and a handler’s gr_result() built with no usage is counted here rather than taken as a reported 0 in and 0 out.

  • Embeddings requests record attempts, served_model and a provenance like any other request; attempts was always NA although they are retried, and a failed one had no provenance. as.data.frame() on a trace gains tokens_reasoning, tokens_cached_in and served_model columns when some request has them, and gr_trace_cost() gains paid_reasoning and paid_cached_in.

  • Cached input can be priced at its own rate. gr_register_model() takes cached_input_usd, gr_estimate_cost() takes cached_input_tokens, and gr_models() shows cached_input_usd_per_1m. A model with no cached rate prices cached input as other input, so every built-in model costs what it did.

  • Runs record who they are for. gr_trace() takes system, owner, run_by, purpose and approved_by, and the new option gr_options(actor = list(...)) sets them for every trace; a field named nowhere is NA. They are written to a saved trace under actor and shown by print() when set.

  • Runs record the options in force when the trace was made, under config, with the R version. The values of api_headers are left out, since they can hold credentials.

  • gr_options() given one named argument whose value is a list now sets that option. It used to read the list as a set of options to restore, which only an unnamed list should be.

Cache and replay keys

  • gr_call() takes a draw_index for the draws of a sampled request: 0, the default, for an ordinary call, and 1, 2, … for repeated draws. Above 0 it is part of the response-cache key, so N identical calls with draw indexes 1 to N are N cached replies; before, a cache returned the first reply N times and anything that compared them saw perfect agreement. A handler finds it in params$draw_index and the trace records it in the step’s params; at 0 neither carries it, so an ordinary call is unchanged.

  • The response-cache key is now harnessr-cache-v3, a SHA-256 hash (64 hex digits) in place of xxhash64. Entries written under the old key (readgpt-cache-v2, by readgpt 0.6.0 and earlier builds of harnessr) are still read for calls with no draw index: a call that finds nothing under its new key is looked up under the old one. The first reply found that way in a session warns once for the cache, with class hr_legacy_key, and gr_cache_stats() has a new column, legacy_hits, that counts them. Old entries are never rewritten, new ones are written under the new key only, and gr_cache_clear() removes both.

  • The replay key is now harnessr-replay-v2, and covers the temperature (once the session default is filled in), the output cap asked for and the JSON schema as well as the messages, model and effort. A replay under another temperature, cap or schema now misses instead of being answered with the recorded replies. Each model step of a trace records its key as replay_key. A step recorded before that is looked up by the old key (readgpt-replay-v1: messages, model and effort), with one hr_legacy_key warning per recording in a session and a count in $stats()$legacy_hits. A replay’s own trace records a reply found that way, or one repeated under on_exhausted = "flag", without a replay_key, so a replay of that trace still goes through the old key, or still runs out of replies. A miss on a prompt recorded for the model at the effort asked for says the temperature, output cap or schema differ, names the recorded settings next to the ones this call asks for, and says which of them differ. Where the schema differs, the recorded cap is given as the cap that was sent, which may be the model’s limit rather than the cap asked for.

  • A replay that runs out of recorded replies is an error. A call past the last reply recorded for its request, or for a draw that was never recorded, raises hr_replay_exhausted. It used to repeat the last reply, so a replay making more calls than the recorded run looked like an exact reproduction. gr_replay_client(on_exhausted = "flag") keeps the old behaviour, counted in $stats()$repeats. A call with a draw_index above 0 is answered with the reply recorded for that draw, or the k-th reply to the request in a recording made without draw indexes.

Limits checked before every request

  • max_calls and max_cost_usd now hold exactly. Every request is checked before it is sent, by the call path itself, against what the run has spent plus the most the request could cost: its prompt at the input price and its output cap (for a reasoning model, the raised cap gr_call() sends) at the output price. The prompt is counted with the JSON schema and extra body fields the request carries and a few tokens of framing per message, then raised by safety_margin, since the provider bills for all of that. A request that could take the run past a limit is not sent. Runs used to stop only once what they had spent reached the limit, so they ended up to one request over it; they now end at or under it, as long as the provider stops each reply at its cap and counts the prompt within that margin of the local tokenizer. A run that leaves its output caps at the model’s limit stops while it still has headroom a smaller cap would have used.

  • A refused request is not a call. It comes back from gr_call() as a failed result with refused = TRUE and an error naming the limit, after a condition of class hr_budget_refused is signalled (catch it to stop instead). It adds nothing to the trace’s calls, steps or spend; the trace lists it in a new refusals field, sets budget_stop and names the limit in stop_reason. Readers and review stages treat it as they treated reaching a limit before: the answer or section is marked partial, and the request is not counted as failed.

  • Every request is checked, not only the ones a reader asked about. Judges, the ensemble’s adjudication, conflict resolution in extract, context and proposition segmentation, claims, outlines, screening, synthesis and embeddings requests all go through the same check, as does any request a custom reader or a script makes with gr_call(). The readers no longer check trace_can_call() themselves. It is kept for custom readers written to the 0.6.0 help page, which still work.

  • A chat model with no registered price is refused while a spending limit is set, with a condition of class hr_unpriced_model. Such a model added nothing to the spend, so the limit never stopped it. gr_read() stops before its first request with an hr_unpriced_model error. Register the model’s prices with gr_register_model(), or set gr_options(allow_unpriced = TRUE); then its requests are sent, still count against max_calls and max_tokens_total, and are priced NA in the trace. gr_mock_client() and replays are never refused for this, and neither are embedding models with no price. An ellmer chat is priced as the model it was built with, whatever a spec names, so a chat on a model with no registered price is refused too; the README and the gr_ellmer_client() example now register its price, and allow a local model to run unpriced.

  • New option max_tokens_total (NULL, off) limits the tokens a run may use: prompts and replies of every call, and text sent to be embedded. A request whose prompt and reply at its cap would pass it is refused with stop_reason "tokens". It is the limit that still bounds a run on an unpriced model under allow_unpriced = TRUE. gr_compare() holds the whole comparison to it, as it does to max_cost_usd.

  • New hr_governor() holds a run’s limits: max_calls, max_cost_usd, max_tokens_total, max_output_tokens (the largest output cap one request may carry; a request with a larger one is refused, not cut down), allowed_models and allow_unpriced. Attach one with the new gr_trace(governor = ) argument; a trace without one reads the limits from gr_options(), as before. The new limits are also options, max_tokens_total, max_output_tokens, allowed_models (all NULL, off) and allow_unpriced (FALSE), so every trace’s config snapshot now lists them. as_json() writes a trace’s refusals and governor when it has any, with allowed_models always as an array. gr_read_many(), gr_claims(), gr_outline() and gr_synthesise(), which keep a trace of their own and fold it into the one they are given, hold their requests to that trace’s governor, less what it has already spent and used in tokens; max_calls stays a limit per document and per stage.

  • A parallel batch cannot pass a limit. Each worker’s items are held to an equal share of the calls and dollars the run has left, and an item its share refused before it sent anything runs again in the calling process, against the run. A batch that the run’s limits cannot cover still runs in the calling process, as before. Batch items make one request each; an item that made more and had a later one refused by its share warns (gr_parallel_share) and does not mark the run as stopped.

JSON replies checked against their schema

  • A JSON reply must fit the schema the request sent. Every call that asks for JSON (screening, claims, outlines, preview plans, rerank, iterative reading, model segmentation, extraction) now checks the reply’s types, enum values and required fields, through nested objects and arrays, before using it. A reply that fails is treated as a reply that did not parse: the reader takes its failure path, and the reply is not cached, so running again asks again. A cached reply that fails is asked again too. It used to be enough for a reply to be a named object, so {"decision": "probably"} was a screening reply and was stored as one. Some replies that used to be read leniently are now failed calls: a screening decision outside include, exclude and unclear (it was read as “unclear”), a text field sent as an array or object in iterative, rerank and gr_screen() (it was joined into one string), and a proposition list sent as an array of arrays (the batch is kept as written). Where a reader reports why a call failed, it now says where the reply broke the schema, as in $.groups[0]: expected array, got 1. gr_extract() still reads each field’s value itself, so “1,204” in an integer field is still 1204 and an undeclared value is still reported as one it could not read; only the shape of its replies is checked.

Embedding scores

  • Comparing vectors of different lengths is an error. Cosine similarity cut both vectors to the shorter length, so a lexical fallback vector scored against an API embedding gave a plausible number from two unrelated spaces. It now stops with an error of class hr_dim_mismatch. The readers already kept the query and the chunks in one space; iterative now also falls back to word overlap for a round whose query came back with no vector.

  • BM25 scoring is faster on many chunks. Document frequency is counted once per query term instead of once per term for every chunk, so the rerank prefilter and the offline retrieve path no longer slow down with the square of the number of chunks. Scores are unchanged.

Parameter schemas, declared calls and reader costs

  • New hr_schema(), hr_param() and hr_validate() state a spec’s parameters once: type, default, range and choices. gr_read_spec(), gr_segment_spec() and gr_ingest_spec() now check their arguments through schemas instead of code of their own. They accept the same values and return the same specs, with the same clamps, defaults and warnings; a clamp warning now also has class hr_param_clamped beside gr_clamped.

  • A value outside the choices of context_order, restate, on_overflow, context_source, ocr or layout is still an error, which now names the setting and has class gr_bad_setting, where it used to be a plain match.arg() error that said 'arg'.

  • Readers and segmenters declare the labels their calls carry. gr_register_reader() and gr_register_segmenter() take a new calls argument, the stems of their calls’ trace labels ("stuff.answer", c("map.answer", "reduce")). gr_readers() and gr_segmenters() list them in a new calls column. A reader or segmenter registered without calls declares its own name, which covers labels such as "longest.answer" for a reader called "longest".

  • An effort map that names no declared call is an error. A name in gr_read_spec(effort =) (and the effort of gr_claims(), gr_outline() and gr_synthesise()) must be a declared stem, a part of one up to a dot ("synthesise", "segment"), or a label under one ("reduce.level1"). Anything else stops with an error of class hr_unknown_effort_key that lists the stems. Such a name used to be accepted and matched no call, so a misspelt c(extrac = "low") sent every extraction call at the provider’s default with nothing said. An effort map that names the calls of a reader or segmenter of your own needs that module registered first, with its labels in calls.

  • A reader states its cost as a function. gr_register_reader() takes a new cost argument, a function of (input_stats, params) returning the new hr_cost(): requests expected and at worst, embedding requests, and what the reader must send. The pre-flight check of gr_read() adds up these functions instead of repeating each built-in reader’s call pattern, and the governor decides from the sum whether the run fits its limits before the first request. The built-in readers’ estimates, the trace’s preflight step and the refusals are unchanged. A registered reader without cost is counted as before, one request per chunk. cost_calls is kept for display only, as the description gr_readers() shows; the pre-flight check never reads it, and it will be retired in a later phase. A cost function may also return a plain list with calls_max and no calls, which is read as both. hr_cost() has a tokens_out_max for a reader whose replies can be billed beyond the reply cap; the check prices every request at input_stats$out_cap, the largest cap the run’s model is sent, and uses tokens_out_max when it is larger.

  • hr_param() with a type or tier it does not know is an error of class gr_bad_setting that names the parameter. A named_map parameter takes a character vector or a list whose elements are all named.

Screening

  • gr_calibrate() computes kappa on kept against excluded. 0.6.0 took kappa over the screener’s three labels (include, unclear, exclude) against the person’s two, so every "unclear" counted as a disagreement, while sensitivity in the same object counted an unclear record as kept. The primary table is now kept (include or unclear) against excluded, the definition sensitivity uses, and $agreement$strict holds strict include against the rest as a secondary table. On the eight-record example in ?gr_calibrate kappa moves from 0.33 to 0.50. The old figure is $kappa_legacy for this release only, and is removed in the next.

  • Kappa is no longer reported alone. Each agreement table carries Cohen’s kappa, PABAK and Gwet’s AC1 with intervals, the prevalence and bias indices, and the class-wise sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV; $agreement$kept$paradox flags a table whose prevalence index is above 0.8 in absolute value, where kappa says more about prevalence than agreement. $decisions holds the 3x2 counts, and print() and the audit report show them with the agreement set. The rate of "unclear" decisions is the existing "deferred to a person" metric, with its interval.

  • The kappa interval is a bootstrap over documents. It is a percentile bootstrap with B = 2000 under a fixed seed, so the same sample gives the same interval and the session’s random stream is untouched; B and the seed are in $agreement$kept$bootstrap. AC1 keeps Gwet’s (2008) variance. Where the screener and the person agree on every record, disagree on every record, or the sample holds fewer than 10 records, the kappa and AC1 intervals are left empty (NA) with a $note saying why, instead of a zero-width interval such as [1.00, 1.00].

  • print() on a calibration now shows the 3x2 counts on every sample, including one drawn from a single stratum. The audit report’s calibration section shows the same counts, and sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV with intervals beside kappa, PABAK and AC1.

  • Unclear records no longer leave a review without a word. A gr_screening gains $forward (the included and unclear records, the set a review reads at full text) and $deferred (the unclear ones). gr_extract(screening) still reads only $included in this release and now warns (class gr_unclear_dropped) when that leaves unclear records out; from the next release it reads $forward. Pass screening$forward to read them now. Passing the vector screening$included gives no such warning: $included stays a plain character vector in this release, and a warning on that path is left to a later release.

  • New gr_resolve() records a person’s decision on a deferred or failed record: who decided, when (in UTC) and why, in the table and as a "screen.resolve" step in the trace. forward, deferred and included are rebuilt, the screener’s own decision is kept in screener_decision, and gr_calibrate() compares against that one, so a person’s correction is not credited to the screener. Duplicates of a resolved record take the same decision. The audit report’s screening table shows the screener’s decision and who resolved each record, when and why.

  • gr_flow() accounts for every screened record. A record with no decision is now counted as “could not be read” only when no screening call was made; one whose call failed, or whose reply was not the form asked for, has a row of its own, “screening call failed”. New rows count the records resolved by a person, the records kept for full text ($forward) and, of those, the ones deferred ($deferred).

Claims and outline

  • gr_claims() and gr_outline() record their calls the way the other review stages do. Each records on a trace of its own and, given trace =, adds its calls to that trace when it finishes, as gr_screen(), gr_extract(), gr_read_many() and gr_synthesise() already did. Before, both recorded straight onto the trace they were given, so a review trace that an earlier stage had taken past gr_options(max_calls =) or max_cost_usd = stopped them before they sent a request, and gr_claims() returned no claims, marked partial. Pass one trace to every stage and its totals are the sum of the stages’, with each request counted once.

  • gr_outline() no longer adds to claims$trace. Given no trace, it recorded its calls on the trace of the claims it was handed, which changed a finished gr_claims() result and made claims$trace report the outline’s cost as the claims’. Its calls are now on attr(outline, "trace"), which gr_outline_pick() keeps and gr_synthesise() keeps as $outline_trace. Scripts that totalled a review’s cost from claims$trace after gr_outline() should pass one trace to both, or add attr(outline, "trace"). The audit report’s claims row still includes the outline’s calls, read from the synthesis, and counts them once when a script passes trace = claims$trace to gr_outline().

Comparing recipes

  • gr_compare() says what each recipe cost. summary gains calls, tokens_in, tokens_out and usd, priced from the requests on the trace at each model’s registered price, and usd_estimated, the share of those dollars spent on requests whose token counts were estimated locally because the provider reported none (NA for a trace whose requests do not record how their counts were obtained, such as one saved by an earlier version). A recipe is charged for a segmentation it shares with an earlier recipe, as it would be run alone, so the column can add up to more than gr_trace_cost(cmp$trace). usd is NA when a model has no registered price. The columns come after error and before premise.

  • gr_compare(correct =) takes strings that a right answer contains (ignoring case and white space) or a function of each gr_answer returning TRUE, FALSE or NA, and adds correct and usd_per_correct, the cost of a right answer: usd when the answer is right, Inf when it is wrong and cost something. Without it the summary has no such columns. A recipe a limit stopped before it found anything is NA, not wrong: the spending, token or call limit, the model allow-list, the output ceiling, or a spending limit refusing a model with no price. A correct function that fails or returns something other than one logical gives a gr_bad_correct warning and NA for that recipe, so the paid results still come back; an invalid correct argument is an error of the same class.

Checking quotations

  • gr_read_spec(verify = TRUE) checks an answer’s quotations against the chunks they come from and lets the check decide what is accepted. gr_read() runs gr_verify_evidence() on the answer, writes its columns onto $evidence, marks the answer partial when a quotation is not found (notes$unverified_evidence), notes how many it checked (notes$quotes_checked) and records a read.verify step in the trace. The iterative reader’s step must then list the passages its answer rests on, word for word with their chunk numbers, and the loop stops only when every one is found in the chunk it names, among those the step was shown. A refused step is told which quotations were not found; a run that ends with none accepted answers NOT_IN_DOCUMENT, keeps the refused answer in notes$unverified_answer and makes no final answer request. Its evidence is the quoted passages, not every chunk it was shown. A refusal is sent back even when retrieval has no unseen chunks left, so the next step can quote what it already has. With premise = TRUE, a step that reports the premise false is not held to quotations in this release and stops the loop as it does without verify. verify = FALSE, the default, sends every request as before, and the field is in the spec only when TRUE, so cache, replay and corpus store keys are unchanged.

  • A second quote matcher is recorded beside verified. Evidence tables that are checked (skim, extract, screen, iterative with verify = TRUE) and gr_verify_evidence() gain quote_status, quote_sim, quote_coverage, quote_edits and quote_critical_ok, from a matcher that expands ligatures, joins words broken across a line with a hyphen, undoes JSON escapes and scores the closest window of the source by character edits, with numbers (in digits or in words, with any comparison sign before them and the unit after), and negations required to be identical. A passage too long to score (its length times the source’s over 5e7 characters) is not_checked. Its statuses are verbatim, near_verbatim (similarity at least 0.90, or 0.95 under 40 characters, five words or more), unverified and not_checked. It decides nothing in this release: verified and match are the existing check’s, as before. On a labelled set of 343 true and 162 false quotations it rejects 1.2% of true ones (95% CI 0.3% to 3.0%) against 36.4% (31.3% to 41.8%) for the existing check, and accepts none of the 52 with a changed digit, 8 with a changed number word, 3 with a changed comparison sign, 37 with a flipped negation or 16 invented sentences; it does accept 25 of 46 quotations with one content word swapped as near_verbatim, which is why that status is not verified. Rscript dev/quote-matcher-rates.R prints the full table.

Trace records of state and cuts

  • refine and hierarchical write the length of the state they carry. Each refine.draft and refine.revise step in the trace gains state$tokens_in (the draft the request carried) and state$tokens_out (the draft carried on from it, which is the old one when the reply was unusable). Each hier.summarise.L<k> step gains the length of the text it summarised and of the summary it returned, the hier.answer step the length of the summaries it was sent, and each level adds a local hier.state.L<k> step with the number of summaries handed on and their combined length. A draft that shrinks sharply in one revision can now be seen in the trace.

  • Every cut writes a truncate step to the trace with where it was made (detail$where: refine.excerpt, refine.draft, hier.summaries, preview.skim, preview.outline, <label>.input for a finding cut to fit a merge, <label>.giveup for the capped findings a failed merge returns, segment.contextual.header, segment.contextual.document, screen.opening, synthesise.gaps, embed.input), the token limit, and the tokens before, kept and dropped (the truncation marker is not counted as kept). For screen.opening the limit is the screening cap on the opening with its heading; for segment.contextual.header it is the room the header was cut to. A preview.skim cut lists the cut section’s chunk_ids, always as a JSON array. refine and hierarchical answers also gain notes$tokens_truncated, and their printed answer now says how many tokens were cut (“N token(s) cut to fit”) when a cut happened. The preview reader’s notes$tokens_truncated is now the tokens a cut dropped rather than the overshoot over the cap, a correction to a count that measured the wrong thing. Requests, cache keys and replay keys are unchanged; the trace of a run that cut nothing gains only the state lengths above.

Conformance checks

  • New gr_check_reader() and gr_check_segmenter() run one registered reader or segmenter on gr_example() through an offline mock client and report which rules of its contract it breaks. A reader is checked for finishing without an error, returning a gr_answer with the fields gr_read() documents and a single string as its answer, evidence and chunks_used that name only chunks of the input, call labels covered by the stems it declared in calls, and no more requests than its cost function’s worst case for that input. A segmenter is checked for finishing without an error, returning a gr_chunks with the documented columns, text in every chunk, unique chunk ids, no chunk over max_tokens that gr_segment() had to split, and call labels covered by its declared stems. Every built-in reader and segmenter passes them.

  • New hr_check_module() is the core helper both use: it runs a closure that calls a module in a temporary working directory, catches its error and warnings, asks a named list of rule functions about what came back, and returns an hr_conformance data frame with a rule, ok and detail for each. ok is NA for a rule that could not be checked. print() lists the broken rules first, says “passes all N rules” when every rule passes, and says “passes all N rules checked; M not checked” when some rules could not be checked.

  • The checks are reports only. gr_register_reader() and gr_register_segmenter() still check only that fn is a function, and register a module that breaks a rule as before.

Fixed

  • A download refused for size no longer breaks the downloads after it. httr shares one curl handle per host, and a stream stopped at the size limit could leave that handle attached to its connection, so every later download from the same host in the session failed with “Handle is already in use elsewhere”. Each request now gets its own handle.

Phase 2

  • New guide, vignette("evaluate") (“Measuring and comparing configurations”), covers reference sets and label sheets, benchmarks and their reports, non-inferiority, judges, baselines, drift and signals; vignette("review") gains recall against a target, the stopping test, several reviewers and agreement on extracted fields.

Agreement and estimation statistics

  • New hr_prop_ci() gives Wilson, Clopper-Pearson or Jeffreys intervals for proportions, vectorised over x and n, two-sided or as a one-sided bound. Wilson matches prop.test(correct = FALSE), including a lower bound of exactly 0 at x = 0 and an upper bound of exactly 1 at x = n (the formula alone left a rounding error there for 38 and 60 of the values of n from 1 to 200, such as a lower bound of 2.8e-17 at 0 of 10), and Clopper-Pearson matches binom.test(). The help says which to use: Wilson for descriptive rates, Clopper-Pearson for any “at least” or “at most” guarantee.

  • New hr_agreement() reports agreement between two raters as the count table with observed agreement, Cohen’s kappa (standard error and a bootstrap interval over items), the prevalence and bias indices, PABAK, Gwet’s AC1 with its variance interval, positive and negative specific agreement, and, when positive is given, sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV against the second rater. paradox_flag marks tables where kappa should not be compared across samples. For a matrix of coders, or a level other than nominal, it reports Krippendorff’s alpha at the nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio level with a bootstrap interval, and reports only percent agreement, with a note, below 30 items or for a constant field. It has print() and as_json() methods, and its bootstrap leaves the caller’s random state as it was. Factor levels that neither rater used are left out of the two-rater table with a note, and a positive label that is not among the labels is an error. When coders’ factors carry different level sets, ordinal alpha merges them keeping each coder’s order (low, high and low, mid, high give low, mid, high), and levels that conflict or leave two levels unordered are an error.

  • New hr_ht_estimate() estimates a total (Horvitz-Thompson), a mean (Hajek) or a ratio of totals from a sample drawn with known inclusion probabilities, optionally stratified, with the difference estimator when predictions for the whole population are given, and a bootstrap interval that resamples within strata with the finite population correction (the Rao-Wu rescaling bootstrap). A stratum judged in full (pi = 1) adds no variance: a census of 20 records gives se 0 and the interval [12, 12] for a total of 12, and a simple random sample of 100 from 200 with 30 eligible gives se 6.5, the design value.

  • New hr_ppi() gives a prediction-powered estimate of a mean from many model-labelled units and a few labelled by people, with the power-tuned PPI++ weight by default and inverse-probability weighting when the labelled units were drawn with unequal probabilities.

  • New hr_alt_test() runs the alternative annotator test of Calderon, Reichart and Dror (2025): whether a model’s labels can be used in place of three or more human annotators, with the margin set by their declared expertise, a Benjamini-Yekutieli correction, the winning rate, and the winning rate over margins from 0.05 to 0.20. Annotator column names must be unique and non-empty.

  • gr_calibrate() and its output are unchanged.

Benchmarks: arms, references, scorers and hr_benchmark()

  • New hr_arm() describes one configuration to compare: a function of an item and a context that carries the client, a trace of the run alone, the governor and the run’s draw_index, with ctx$call() as a shortcut for gr_call() that fills in all three. run is required. The arm records its settings, a version and a hash of its code and settings, which is the same in every session and after saveRDS(), also for an arm built inside a function of yours. The hash covers the values the code reads from where it was written, the workspace included, so an arm at top level that reads a global prompt gets a new hash when the prompt changes.

  • New hr_reference() holds the items to score, their labels, clusters, splits ("dev", "exploratory", "calibration", "test", "final"), inclusion probabilities, strata and coder labels, with a content hash. Labels, clusters, splits, inclusion probabilities and strata given with names are matched to the items by name (c(q2 = "Lima", q1 = "Paris") gives q1 Paris), and names that are not the item ids are an error of class hr_bad_reference. Items can be added with hr_reference_add() until a benchmark starts scoring the reference; after that every copy of it, and every reference grown from it, refuses new items with an error of class hr_reference_locked.

  • New hr_scorer() states the scoring contract (correct, outcome and failure kind for each run), and hr_scorer_exact(), the default, compares text after folding case and white space, and sorts parse failures, errors, NOT_IN_DOCUMENT and failures an arm reports itself apart from wrong answers. A number in a label is compared in plain digits, so the label 100000 accepts "100000".

  • New hr_benchmark() runs every arm on every item of the chosen splits runs times (5 by default; fewer warns) and returns one row per cluster x item x arm x run with correctness, failure kind, tokens by kind, cost and its provenance, seconds, the draw index and the id of the run’s trace. Run r is draw r, so repeated runs are separate cache entries and recorded draws, and an arm whose runs come back as one stored reply (the same cache entry, a repeated replay, a repeated response id) is refused with an error of class hr_duplicate_draw. Each draw is also recorded under the arm’s name, and gr_replay_client() answers an arm only with its own replies, so replaying some of the arms, or the arms in another order, gives each arm what it got even when two arms sent the same request. The whole benchmark is held to one governor; a run with a refused request is recorded as a budget stop and counted wrong, and the benchmark warns (class hr_budget_stopped) with the number of runs stopped, the limits that stopped them, how many count against an arm, and the first run stopped. With no governor the limits are gr_options()’s, set for one run of a reader (400 calls), and the warning gives the values of the options that stopped runs and, for a call, spending or token limit, says to pass a governor sized for the benchmark. A reader stopped by its own check before its first request now leaves a budget.preflight note on the run’s trace naming the limit, and the errors that check raises carry the limit in $limit. Every run on an item with no label has correct = NA, failures included, so such an item never counts against an arm. Rows on the dev split are marked not reportable. print() shows accuracy per arm over the reportable rows and labelled items, with the dev split’s accuracy in its own column, descriptive only.

Benchmark reports: hr_report()

  • New hr_report() turns the reportable rows of an hr_benchmark() into accuracy per arm (mean over runs within each item, then over items) with intervals that keep clusters together. With the default method = "auto" and at least 300 items and 30 clusters it uses method = "bootstrap", which is now a studentised (bootstrap-t) cluster bootstrap rather than BCa: it resamples whole clusters with all their items, runs and arms (B = 2000, or 5000 with confirmatory = TRUE), each resample studentised by its own linearised standard error. Below either threshold it uses the new method = "cluster_t", a cluster-robust t interval on the logit scale: the linearised variance of the ratio estimator with the C / (C - 1) factor and t quantiles on C - 1 degrees of freedom (Cameron and Miller 2015). Both can be asked for at any size. Where neither is defined (accuracy 0 or 1, or the same in every cluster) the arm gets Korn and Graubard’s interval, one-sided from the bound at 0 or 1, with a note. method = "exact" gives Clopper-Pearson on the effective number of items from cluster totals (Korn and Graubard) instead, with items rather than runs as trials, and method = "bayes" a Bayesian beta-binomial model with a cluster random effect and flat priors, with a note on its calibration. No interval treats items or runs as independent trials.

    These methods replace the BCa cluster bootstrap and the Bayesian model as defaults after the coverage simulation (dev/sim-coverage.R, 2000 replicates) failed them: BCa covered 93.5% for accuracy at 0.75 and 92.9% for the paired difference with 40 clusters, and 89.2% for the difference with 10 clusters; the Bayesian model covered 96.5% to 96.6% with 10 clusters, its misses 2.9% to 3.2% below the truth and 0.2% to 0.5% above. With the new methods the same simulation passes: accuracy 95.5% and 95.0%, difference 94.7% with 40 clusters; accuracy 95.8% and 95.7%, difference 95.7% with 10 clusters.

  • The report also gives paired differences between arms (every pair, or the ones in contrasts) with cluster-robust t intervals on C - 1 degrees of freedom at every size, cut to [-1, 1] (when every cluster gives the same mean difference, so the cluster variance is 0, Tango’s score interval with the items as pairs and the item count scaled for C - 1 degrees of freedom, with a note), single-step max-t simultaneous intervals over all pairs from the multivariate t with the same correlation (Hothorn, Bretz and Westfall 2008), and bootstrap rank intervals in place of a ranking by point estimate. A pair whose cluster variance is 0 takes Tango’s interval at the Bonferroni share (1 - conf) / number of pairs, and the max-t critical value over the rest is then taken at 1 - (1 - conf) x (pairs with variance above 0) / (number of pairs), so the family stays at conf: with 3 pairs, one at variance 0, and 12 clusters it is 2.43, where the full-level 2.20 left the family at up to 6.7% error. The critical column is NA on the Tango rows. print() shows the simultaneous interval of a contrast written against benchmark order (b - a) as the negated interval of its pair, [-upper, -lower], where it printed “-”; flip rate, TARa and run-level SD; pass^k with the unbiased estimator; dollars and tokens per item and per correct item with intervals, flagging arms whose cost rests on estimated token counts for more than 5%; the cost-accuracy frontier with each arm’s share of resamples on it; failure counts with accuracy recomputed without parse failures and refusals; and within-item and between-item variance on the probability scale, with a note to use 10 runs when runs account for more than 10%. Below 5 runs the report is descriptive only, without intervals. An item scored on some runs but not all is refused. It has print() and as_json() methods and leaves the caller’s random state as it was. The help writes its intervals with their brackets, such as [r - q_hi se, r - q_lo se] and “cut to [0, 1]”; they had been turned into 5 broken links, which R CMD check reported as a warning and the rendered help showed without brackets. The BCa intervals still used for cost and pass^k count a resample as below t0 only when it is more than 1e-12 x max(1, |t0|) below it, so a resample that ties with t0 up to a rounding error is not counted. This is the count in exact arithmetic; boot.ci() counts sum(t < t0) and can differ when there are such ties (484 against 495 of 999 resamples in one test, moving the limits by less than 0.001).

Non-inferiority contrasts and the minimum detectable difference

  • New hr_mdd() and hr_n_needed() give the smallest paired accuracy difference a clustered design can detect, and the items needed for a given one, from n_eff = (t_(C - 1, 1 - alpha’) + t_(C - 1, power))^2 x p_disc / Delta^2 with t quantiles on C - 1 degrees of freedom for C clusters, the degrees of freedom of the report’s non-inferiority bound, and the design effect DE = 1 + (m - 1) x ICC_D, where ICC_D is the intra-cluster correlation of the paired item difference and m becomes (cv^2 + 1) x m for unequal clusters. With n_contrasts above 1, alpha’ is alpha / n_contrasts, the first step of Holm. For 480 questions in 80 documents at ICC_D 0.2 and p_disc 0.2 this gives DE 2, 240 effective items and an MDD of 8.2 points, or 10.7 points after Holm over nine contrasts (8.1 and 10.4 with normal quantiles). hr_n_needed() finds the number of items by root finding, since the degrees of freedom depend on it, and both refuse a design of one cluster. hr_n_needed() also takes a true difference below 0. Its print() rounds the clusters up first and gives the items as that many clusters of m: 840 items in 140 clusters of 6 for n_items 837.8, where it printed 838 items, not a multiple of 6.

  • New hr_contrast() and hr_register_contrasts() fix non-inferiority contrasts (arm, reference arm, margin, whether it must also be cheaper) against an hr_reference() before a benchmark scores it. A confirmatory margin below the design MDD at 80% power after Holm is refused with an error of class hr_margin_below_mdd; with confirmatory = FALSE it is registered as exploratory. The check is at one-sided alpha 0.025 or less whatever level the design was given at, and a design with more items or clusters than the reference holds on the test and final splits is refused. A reference already being scored, or one rebuilt with the same content, is refused (hr_registration_after_scoring), and the registration is hashed. hr_mdd() takes whole numbers of items and clusters only.

  • hr_report() gains registration. Each registered contrast is non-inferior only if the one-sided lower bound of the accuracy difference is above -margin and, when it tests cost, the upper bound of the paired cost difference (BCa cluster bootstrap) is below 0. The accuracy bound is the cluster-robust t bound of the report’s paired differences, taken one-sided on C - 1 degrees of freedom (the Tango bound with items as pairs when every cluster gives the same mean difference), so at one-sided 0.025 it is the lower end of the printed 95% contrast interval. It replaces the BCa cluster bootstrap bound, which undercovered the paired difference in the coverage simulation (92.9% with 40 clusters, 89.2% with 10). Confirmatory contrasts are tested with Holm’s step-down procedure, exploratory ones at alpha. The design and achieved MDD are printed beside every verdict (the achieved one on the linearised standard error and the same t quantiles as hr_mdd(), and NA when the cluster variance is 0), and a contrast that passed its registered test is reported as passed even when the achieved MDD exceeds its margin. Tango’s (1998) paired score interval on effective counts, at most one pair per item, is given as a cross-check. A changed registration, or one for another reference, is refused. Each contrast’s p_value is the smallest one-sided level at which it passes, found by bisection down to 1e-6. With a cost test the search stops at 1 / (B + 1) (1 / 2001, about 5.0e-4, at B = 2000): below that level the BCa cost bound is the most extreme resample and stops moving, and a contrast whose resamples were all cheaper was reported at 1e-6 where a cluster t on the paired cost means gave 2.3e-4.

  • Dev-split rows are refused as evidence. A report with a registration or confirmatory = TRUE errors with class hr_dev_not_evidence when the benchmark holds rows on the dev, exploratory or calibration split or rows marked not reportable.

Benchmarking reading recipes

  • New gr_arm() and gr_arms() wrap reading recipes as benchmark arms. Each run reads the item’s document with answer_document(), or with gr_read() when the document is already chunked, and returns the gr_answer, with every request on the run’s own trace. That trace gives every request of the run, segmenter and reader requests included, the run’s draw index, so repeated runs under a cache or a recording are separate draws. A reader that refuses to start because the run’s call or spending limit leaves too little returns a partial NOT_IN_DOCUMENT answer noting the limit, which is scored as a budget stop rather than an error. The arm records the recipe and its settings, and its version is the package version.

  • New gr_qa_reference() builds an hr_reference() of questions about documents from questions, documents and acceptable answers (one string or a list of alternatives per question). Unanswerable questions, given as flags, ids, positions or the answer NOT_IN_DOCUMENT, are labelled NOT_IN_DOCUMENT. The payload an arm is given holds the question and the document only: whether an item is unanswerable is in its label. Items are clustered by document by default.

  • New gr_scorer_answer() marks an answer right when it contains an accepted answer after folding case, white space and thousands separators ("1,204" matches "1204"), with numbers matched whole ("12" is not in ".12" or "-12", but is in "12-15", and "45.2" is in "45.2m"), a numeric label written in plain digits, and an unanswerable item right when is_not_found() is true and no limit or refusal stopped the run. Wrong answers are sorted into parse failures, budget stops, refusals, not_in_document and wrong.

  • gr_compare()’s help now says it is descriptive, and points to hr_benchmark() and hr_report() for a comparison with intervals.

Judges and their validation record

  • New hr_judge() asks a model to choose between candidates ("select"), compare two ("pairwise") or grade one against a reference ("grade"). Candidates are shown under the letters A, B, … only, and each item is asked in two presentation orders: reversed for candidates, reference first and then response first for grading. A verdict that differs between the orders, mapped back to the candidate it names, is returned as "unresolved" with degradation = "judge_inconsistent"; a failed request or a reply with no allowed verdict is "failed". One order is allowed for grading only. With more than two candidates, orders above 2 shows cyclic rotations. Requests go through the same path as gr_call(), so the governor, a cache keyed with draw_index and the trace all apply, under the labels judge.<mode>.o<k>. They are recorded in the judge’s own trace and their cost in $judge_cost, never in the trace of the run being judged, which gets a local note pointing at the judge’s trace; the judge is held to what that run’s governor has left.

  • New hr_judge_config() holds what decides a judge’s answers (model, mode, rubric, the package’s instructions for the mode, reply schema, orders, how verdicts are combined, the positive grade) with a SHA-256 hash of them.

  • New hr_judge_validate() and hr_judge_valid(). From blind human labels on a judge’s decisions, the record gives Cohen’s kappa with a bootstrap interval and the full hr_agreement() set, sensitivity and specificity with Wilson intervals (and the sensitivity half-width), and the swap-inconsistency rate. Items the judge left unresolved or failed on count as not called positive, the rule hr_scorer_judge() applies, so the figures describe the judge as the scorer uses it. Fewer than 50 human-positive or 50 human-negative items are refused with hr_judge_too_few_labels, and the minimums cannot be lowered. Text labels such as "pass" and "fail" default to the configuration’s positive grade. A judge column that shares no value with human (logical calls beside "pass"/"fail" labels) is refused with gr_bad_setting rather than counted as all negative. The optional columns consistent, outcome and config_hash are read by exact name, so an extra column such as consistently_long is ignored. The record is keyed by the configuration hash; hr_judge_valid() is FALSE, naming what changed, when the model, rubric, prompt, schema, orders, aggregation or positive grade differ, or when the record was edited.

  • New hr_scorer_judge(), a benchmark scorer that grades each output against its label with a grade-mode judge. It refuses to be built without a valid record (hr_judge_unvalidated). Unresolved judgements count as wrong and failed ones as errors, and the judge’s requests stay in the scorer’s own trace, out of the benchmark’s cost columns. A draw_index argument sets the cache draw for the judge’s requests.

  • New hr_judge_ppi() corrects judge-scored accuracy with human labels on a sample through hr_ppi(): prediction-powered inference, and the inverse-probability weighted DSL form when the labelling probabilities vary. It also reports the uncorrected judge mean. Its normal interval needs enough labelled items in every inclusion stratum; with few labels at small inclusion probabilities it is too narrow.

Baselines without a model

  • New hr_tfidf() turns texts into an l2-normalised tf-idf matrix: lower-cased runs of letters and digits, terms in at least min_df texts (at most max_features, the most frequent), raw counts times the smoothed idf log((1 + n) / (1 + df)) + 1. It is a dense base R matrix, which suits a reference or screening set of a few thousand texts.

  • New hr_baseline_classifier(), a ridge-penalised logistic regression on tf-idf features fitted by iteratively reweighted least squares and cross-fitted by fold, so each item is predicted by a model that never saw it. Folds are stratified by label, or keep each cluster whole. The vocabulary and idf are fitted on each training fold only. More than two labels are fitted one against the rest. It returns the out-of-fold probabilities and labels, the training size of each fold, and accuracy with a Wilson interval from hr_prop_ci().

  • New hr_baseline_ranker() simulates prioritised screening over a fully labelled set, as ASReview does: it starts from seed_n relevant and irrelevant records, refits after each batch, and screens the record with the highest predicted relevance next. The model is the same ridge logistic regression or multinomial naive Bayes. It returns the screening order, the recall curve, the records screened to reach 95% recall, WSS@95 and the number a random order would need on average.

  • New gr_stop_test(), the hypergeometric stopping test of Callaghan and Muller-Hansen (2020) for prioritised screening. After each screened record it gives the p-value for recall still being below target given the records left unscreened, and the first point where screening may stop at alpha. It takes a vector of relevance in screening order, with unscreened records as trailing NA, or an hr_baseline_ranker() result.

Drift checks

  • New hr_drift_check() reruns an arm live on the items of a frozen hr_benchmark() and reports, item by item, which items were lost, gained or moved, with their most common output before and after. Two tests are fixed in the call, with alpha and an optional alert threshold. (a) The accuracy change, live minus frozen, by a BCa cluster bootstrap over documents on paired item accuracy, with the clustered McNemar test of Obuchowski (1998) beside it as a cross-check. (b) Excess instability: the flips between frozen and live runs against the flips among replicate runs, frozen and live, one-sided, on the same cluster resamples. Per item it estimates the squared change in accuracy, so it sees losses and gains that cancel in accuracy and noisy items that turn deterministic; it needs at least 2 live runs. The alert is crossed when the whole accuracy interval lies beyond the threshold, and alert_not_ruled_out reports the weaker reading, an interval that reaches beyond it. Moved items whose runs disagreed are counted apart in the printout, since their moves can be run-to-run variation. Fewer than 5 frozen runs is refused (hr_drift_few_runs), as are a changed arm, another reference or scorer (hr_drift_mismatch) and a live rerun answered from a cache or a recording (hr_drift_not_live). The live rerun is returned as an hr_bench.

Validation of the intervals and the MDD

  • A nightly validation job checks the report’s statistics on simulated benchmarks. dev/sim-coverage.R simulates clustered corpora with a known effect, document ICC and run variance, reports each with hr_report(), and gives the coverage of the accuracy and paired difference intervals over 2000 replicates with its Wilson 95% interval, in a large design (386 items in 40 clusters, studentised cluster bootstrap) and a small one (50 items in 10 clusters, cluster-robust t on the logit scale, with the Korn-Graubard interval beside it). An interval passes when that Monte Carlo interval contains 95% and its lower end is at least 93%. dev/sim-power.R sets hr_mdd() against a power simulation of the report’s cluster-robust t non-inferiority bound and passes when the simulated MDD is within 1 point. Both exit with status 1 on a failure. The workflow .github/workflows/validation.yaml runs them every night and by hand, never on pull requests, and keeps the printed tables as an artifact. The power table’s power_check column also marks a design whose simulated power at the formula’s MDD lies below or above the target beyond Monte Carlo error (“below target” or “above target”), without failing the run.

  • The hr_mdd() help gives the power simulation’s result (2000 replicates, seed 1): the MDD was 0.16 and 0.17 points below the simulated one at 80 equal clusters (simulated power at the formula’s MDD 78.55% and 78.30%) and 0.25 points above it at 40 unequal clusters (81.60%). With normal quantiles it was 0.26 and 0.41 points below at 80 clusters (power 77.20% and 76.05%, short of 80% beyond Monte Carlo error), which is why the formula takes t quantiles.

Screening recall against a target

  • gr_reference(of = "stacked") draws the reference the screening help recommends in one sheet: every record the screener kept, and n of those it excluded. Each row records its stratum and its inclusion probability (1 for a kept record, n / N for an excluded one). A blind sheet keeps both inside a key per row of one length, so they do not reveal what the model decided. frame = is accepted as another name for of. The other frames draw exactly as before.

  • gr_calibrate() estimates recall on a stacked reference instead of refusing it: the ratio of Horvitz-Thompson totals, K / (K + M), with M the projected number of eligible records excluded and exact hypergeometric bounds on M mapped into a one-sided lower bound on recall. A kept sheet and an excluded sheet stacked with rbind() are read the same way with of = "stacked"; without it they are still refused.

  • gr_calibrate() gains recall_target (0.95), conf (0.95) and max_lost, and its result gains recall, lost, false_exclusion, work_saved, unclear_rate, strata and verdict, which says whether the one-sided lower bound on recall reaches the target (or the bound on M is within max_lost). A sample of everything screened bounds recall with Clopper-Pearson, except that when it is every screened record recall is known exactly and is its own bound (method = "census": 25 of 25 eligible kept gives a bound of 1, not the 0.887 Clopper-Pearson gives); a sample of the exclusions alone bounds M but not recall. Every field it returned before is unchanged.

  • New gr_screen_sample_size() gives the reference size a recall target needs: n >= ln(alpha) / ln(T) eligible records with no miss (59 for 95% at 95% confidence), divided by prevalence for the records to draw, and for a sample of the exclusions the exact hypergeometric size for a frame of frame_n records with at most max_lost lost, beside the binomial one. For a sample of everything screened, giving frame_n with prevalence caps the draw at the frame: a frame of 500 records at 5% prevalence holds about 25 eligible records, fewer than the 59 needed, so n is 500 (judge every record) rather than 1180. A smaller draw cannot pass gr_calibrate(), which bounds such a sample with Clopper-Pearson: 388 records with 22 eligible and none missed give a bound of 0.873.

References from several reviewers

  • gr_reference(reviewers = k) writes one decision column per reviewer, human_decision_1 to human_decision_<k>, and a consensus column for an adjudicator, one row per document. With one reviewer the sheet is as before.

  • New gr_reference_consensus() forms one decision per document from several reviewers, by rule = "majority" (a tie is settled by consensus where filled, and otherwise settled as include), "any_include" or "adjudicated" (the consensus column, an error where reviewers disagree and it is empty). It also reads a long sheet with a reviewer column. Each row says in consensus_from how its decision was reached. Columns named human_decision_<x> are reviewers, except those ending in _note, _notes, _comment, _comments or _date.

  • gr_calibrate() compares the screener with the reviewers’ consensus on a multi-reviewer sheet, and stops only on a disagreement nobody settled, saying how many there were. Its result gains reviewers: agreement between each pair of reviewers from hr_agreement() (kappa beside PABAK, AC1 and the prevalence and bias indices, never alone), Krippendorff’s alpha with three reviewers or more, and each reviewer’s sensitivity and specificity against the consensus. On a stacked reference both are weighted by the stratum weights recall uses, with exact hypergeometric bounds for the rates and a bootstrap within the sampled stratum for agreement; the notes flag the weighted kappa interval as approximate when fewer than 100 excluded records were sampled. A one-reviewer calibration is unchanged.

Agreement on extracted fields

  • New gr_extract_agreement() compares two extraction tables for the same documents, a model’s gr_extract() result against a person’s or two people’s, matched on document. Each field gets Krippendorff’s alpha at a declared level (levels =; by default interval for integer and number fields and nominal otherwise) with a bootstrap interval over documents, percent agreement and the number of documents compared. “Not reported” is a category of its own in a nominal field; an ordinal, interval or ratio field gets a separate row for agreement on whether it is reported, and its value row covers the documents both tables report. Below 30 documents or for a constant field alpha is NA and a note says why. Rows of a gr_extract() result that failed or were read only in part are not taken as reporting nothing, duplicates are left out (a blank duplicate_of, as a table saved with write.csv(na = "") reads back, is not a duplicate), and $pairs lists every cell side by side for reading the disagreements.

Signals, calibration records and gate thresholds

  • New hr_signal() and hr_signals(). hr_signal() records a value the package produced about its own work (a self-signal) into a trace, as a local step labelled "signal"; it sends no request, so requests and cache keys are unchanged. hr_signals() reads every recorded signal back from a trace, an answer or a list of them as one table, a row per value, with the value as text and as a number. A trace object reached twice in the list is read once; two separate traces are both read even when they share a run_id (two traces made with gr_trace(run_id = "pilot") give 2 rows, not 1).

  • Three readers record a signal. iterative records gr.iterative.can_answer for each step whose reply parsed, preview records gr.preview.skip for each section of a usable plan (the plan’s own decision, before any section is demoted to skim), and ensemble records gr.ensemble.adjudicate as "model", "concatenated" or "single member". No reader behaves differently: each answer, each request and each cache key is as before, and a trace from these readers has one more local step per signal.

  • New hr_calibrate_signal() measures a signal against a graded set that must include unanswerable items, on the half of each cluster’s items not used to fit the map: the Brier score with its reliability, resolution and uncertainty decomposition (and the two within-bin terms that make it exact over binned forecasts), type-2 AUROC, the area under the risk-coverage curve with the selective risk at 50, 80 and 90 percent coverage, and the debiased equal-mass calibration error over 5 to 10 bins, each with a cluster bootstrap interval (NA when the calibration half has one cluster, with a note below 20 clusters). AUROC and the risk-coverage curve are taken on the signal itself, so a signal that is higher when the item is wrong shows an AUROC below 0.5 even after the map turns it round. The map is Platt scaling, isotonic regression (only from 1000 graded items, counted before the split) or none. A map that does not increase with the signal keeps the record advisory. The record is keyed by served model, model version, task, format, prompt hash, effort, module and contract version, starts advisory, says why, and has print() and as_json() methods.

    The ECE and the Brier decomposition use the same bins, and items with the same p always share one, so the ECE does not depend on row order. A signal with two values on 200 documents of 10 items, calibrated within each value, had an ECE of 0.044 that fell to 0 when its rows were shuffled; it is now 0 either way. bins is the number of bins formed: 2 for a logical signal, which therefore stays advisory under the 5-bin rule (it reported 10). A graded set with a split column is calibrated on its calibration rows alone, with the rows left out counted in notes and a message (before, dev, exploratory and test rows were fitted and scored too), and one with no calibration row stops with hr_bad_calibration. Columns are read by exact name, so a cluster_size column is no longer taken for cluster (40 documents of 10 items collapsed to 1 cluster).

  • New hr_calibration_valid() is FALSE when any key field of a record differs from the run’s, and names the fields.

  • New hr_gate_threshold() picks a threshold by Learn-then-Test: the thresholds are tested from strict to loose with a one-sided Clopper-Pearson bound on the error among accepted items, or on the miss rate for exclusions, and the loosest one before the first failure is kept. The bound is taken on an effective sample, n / deff items with k / deff errors, where the design effect deff is the cluster variance of the error rate over the variance with each item its own cluster, never below 1. Taken at face value, items from one document are not independent: with 30 documents of 20 items, a true error rate of 0.12 and an intraclass correlation of 0.3, a gate at alpha = 0.10 and delta = 0.05 passed in 8.7 percent of draws; it now passes in 2.4 percent. Unclustered items give deff = 1 and the exact Clopper-Pearson bound. $gate reports deff and n_eff, and $gate$path the deff of every threshold. It starts where enough items are acted on for the bound to reach alpha, and reports "none passed" or "too few items" when nothing qualifies. A record becomes "gating" only with a passing threshold, at least 100 wrong items in the graded set, a map that increases with the signal and an ECE over at least 5 bins.

  • New hr_signal_policy() and hr_apply_signal(). A signal gates its action only with a gating record for the same signal and action whose key matches the run; otherwise it stays advisory (gated = FALSE), the item is routed to a check, a person or nowhere, and reason says why. Nothing in the package calls hr_apply_signal() yet, so nothing gates by default.

Splits and label sheets

  • New hr_assign_splits() assigns reference items to the dev, exploratory, calibration, test and final splits by cluster, so every item of a document lands in the same split. The default shares are 10% dev, 10% exploratory, 30% calibration and 50% test. Each cluster’s place comes from the SHA-256 digest of the seed and its id, so the assignment does not depend on row order or the session’s random state. With method = "stable" (the default) adding or dropping documents never moves another one; method = "balanced" gives each split its share of clusters by largest remainders. The result reports clusters and items per split beside the target shares, and warns with hr_empty_split when a split given a share receives nothing. A whole-number cluster id is hashed written in full, so document 300000 gets the same split stored as a double or as an integer (as a double it was hashed as "3e+05" and went to test instead of calibration with seed 7). Columns are matched by exact name: a frame with no item_id, id or cluster column no longer takes ideal_answer for its ids or cluster_size for its clusters.

  • New gr_label_sheet() writes a CSV for people to label, with an instructions file beside it, for five kinds of set: QA answers, a screening reference, extraction fields, a calibration graded set and judge validation verdicts. Each row has an item_id and empty decision columns. A blind sheet (the default) copies only the columns a person needs to judge the item, so no model output or sampling detail reaches it. With several reviewers each gets a sheet of their own. The help page gives the number of items each set needs for the package’s own evaluation. Ids come from a column named exactly item_id or id: a frame whose only such column was ideal_answer used to put the reference answers in the item_id column of a blind sheet; it now gets qa-0001, qa-0002, and so on.

  • New gr_read_labels() reads filled sheets back, checks every value and id, and stops with gr_bad_labels naming the sheet, row and item of each value it cannot read. It returns a screening reference that gr_calibrate() and gr_reference_consensus() take, an extraction table for gr_extract_agreement(), and calibration labels with clusters, with the items’ own columns joined back by id (an item column named like a decision, such as the model’s answer or a judge’s verdict, comes back as model_<name>). Only a calibration sheet written with blind = FALSE has the correct column hr_calibrate_signal() needs; a blind one gives reference answers, and the model’s answers are scored against them to make correct. A blind = FALSE calibration sheet read back without items turns its model_score column back into the number score, so it is a graded set either way (before, only the read with items was). A blind screening sheet carries the reference’s frame as an opaque key, so it reads back as a usable reference without items.
